summary:
Malaysia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at federal and state level. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, for any person regardless of gender or consent; the maximum penalty is 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping, which Human Rights Watch records as mandatory. The offence reaches foreign nationals and tourists, and sodomy was first criminalised in 1871. Section 377D adds "gross indecency", an undefined offence carrying up to two years that remains a discretionary prosecutorial tool.

Every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia enactments criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity, including provisions against "a man posing as a woman". These apply only to Muslims, with penalties of up to three years, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes. Since the 1980s all 13 states passed such enactments; all 13 bar Muslim men from dressing as women and three also bar women posing as men, enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. The Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 are named examples. The High Court denied a challenge to the cross-dressing prohibition's constitutionality. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code.

Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, but raids on queer spaces are documented and current. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest such raid since 2022; media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, and 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point, including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December 2025 the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Earlier raids include a Kuala Lumpur gay bar in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, 11 shopping malls in May 2023 over Swatch Pride watches, and in November 2024 Kelantan approved amendments to its entertainment law banning activities promoting LGBTQ behaviour.

State-sanctioned targeting of trans people is documented. In July 2020 Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons; the International Commission of Jurists condemned the order and demanded its revocation. In 2021, 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt Nur Sajat over "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content were censored.

Violence against trans women is documented with police mistreatment and impunity. A transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb, in a report of 25 June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 2019; no later instance is documented. In June 2014, 16 trans women were mass-arrested at a wedding, triggering the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge. Documented abuse by religious officials includes the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria and repeated arrests of one woman over 20 times. Prison terms of four months to three years carry male-ward sexual violence.

Identity documents are a live battleground. In August 2016 the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered the National Registration Department (NRD) to update a trans man's identity card with his gender identity and chosen name, reasoning that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity as a male; this judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The Registration Department routinely rejects gender-marker changes. The only successful documented gender-marker change is historical: in 1975 NRD recognised Sari Kartina binti Abdul Karim (formerly Mohd Fauzi bin Abdul Karim) as female, and the Johor Deputy Mufti allowed her to marry under sharia law. A 1982 National Fatwa Council edict holds sex is determined at birth and unchanged by sex reassignment surgery, ending domestic sex-reassignment surgery for Muslims; it was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but the 1982 fatwa also bars Muslims from sex reassignment surgery unless intersex and ruled marriages involving transgender people invalid.

Sharia courts may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months (Federal Territories s.56, Kedah s.52, Selangor s.54, Sarawak s.53) and may order cross-dressing or other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution: up to six months in Kelantan (s.19-20) and Pahang (s.66), extended to up to one year by Terengganu's 2022 amendment.

There is no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; the source states plainly there are no Malaysian laws protecting the LGBTQ community against discrimination and hate crimes. Same-sex couples have no route to recognition, and at Cambridge Union in June 2019 Mahathir Mohamad said Malaysia cannot accept same-sex marriage. Hate speech rules do cover orientation: the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Content Code 2022, s.6.1(ii), defines hate speech as material denigrating a person on grounds including sexual orientation, enforced via s.211 of the Communications and Multimedia Act. In 1994 the government banned anyone homosexual, bisexual or transsexual from state-controlled media. Human Rights Watch reports trans people face discriminatory denial of health care and employment alongside arbitrary arrest, physical and sexual assault, and imprisonment. Conversion therapy is practiced regularly and openly promoted by politicians and religious leaders. The National Blood Centre prohibits homosexuals and bisexuals from donating blood, in a policy that appears gender neutral. Adoption is orientation-neutral under the Adoption Act 1952 and Registration of Adoption Act 1952, with no restriction on a single person adopting regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.

On entry, the only stated policy is a 2001 statement by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay and warning gay foreign ministers not to bring their partners; there is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors. In July 2023 the band The 1975 was forced to cut short its Good Vibes Festival set after Matty Healy criticised the country's anti-LGBTQ laws and kissed a bandmate.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch's 10 August 2022 report "I Don't Want to Change Myself", based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers, documents state-backed discrimination. Reuters reported on 21 August 2023 that LGBT people in Malaysia face growing fears as Islamist opposition forecloses reform. The Human Dignity Trust profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise and lists active litigation alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia. The International Commission of Jurists' July 2020 intervention and the Human Rights Law Centre's case summary on the cross-dressing challenge show sustained legal advocacy without a change in the operative prohibitions.

Raw counts of incidents in this record track population and reporting, not per-capita risk: the 208 arrests in the November 2025 Chow Kit raid are a single-operation figure, and the ranking of that raid as the largest since 2022 is by raw count only. The three trans women killed in fewer than two months to June 2019 is a raw count without a denominator in the source.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Home Minister's 2 December 2025 suggestion of revisiting section 377B has produced any legislative or prosecutorial change is unresolved in this record; no subsequent amendment is sourced.

The current operational status of the 1982 fatwa as applied by the Registration Department to gender-marker applications is not sourced beyond the 2017 appellate overturn of the single favourable judgment.

No youth-specific health-care or medication-carrying finding appears in the sources; that question is not sourced here.

The sources give no explicit visa or entry rule for transgender visitors; the only entry policy stated is the 2001 statement on gay foreign ministers and diplomats, whose current force is unresolved.

Human Rights Watch reports discriminatory denial of health care and employment for trans people, but no trans-specific health-care refusal incident with a date is documented in this inventory.

A joint United Nations Development Programme and Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia is listed as a source but its specific findings are not itemised in this inventory.
